title: Journaling with fixed fields
teaches: Log every trade in the same fixed fields: the plan before the click (date, reason, entry, initial stop, target, size), the result after the close (exit, R, how closely you followed the plan, one lesson), emotion and mistake tags from a short fixed list, and a chart saved at entry, so your trades can be sorted and reviewed instead of reread.

facts.quote: As you enter each trade, record your comments about why you made the trade
facts.claim: Write down why you took the trade as you enter it.

facts.quote: include details such as: Price targets Entry and exit points Time of trade Support and resistance levels Technical indicators

facts.quote: If you win a trade, then you want to know exactly why and how. More importantly, you want to know the same when you lose, so you don't repeat unnecessary mistakes.
facts.claim: You want the why and how of your winners as well as your losers.

facts.quote: After each trading day, adding up your profit or loss is secondary to knowing the why and how of your trading performance.
facts.claim: The day's P&L total matters less than knowing why and how you traded.

facts.quote: Be sure to save your trading records so you can go back and analyze elements such as: Profit or loss for a particular system or trading strategy
facts.claim: Keep records so you can check the profit or loss of each strategy.

facts.quote: It sets out the steps you should follow to analyze your trade before you make it and after you close it out. You can start by filling out the sheet for each trade you make.

facts.quote: Record your trades in a trading journal. Review your activities at the end of the month or quarter, and ask yourself the following questions: Were my entries, stops, and exits performed effectively?
facts.claim: Log your trades, then review whether your entries, stops and exits were carried out well.

facts.quote: You can calculate a win/loss ratio by determining the percentage of your trades that have been profitable versus those that haven't.
facts.claim: A win rate is the share of your trades that made money versus those that didn't.

facts.quote: Stock Trade Plan Worksheet Date:
facts.claim: Schwab's worksheet starts with the date.

facts.quote: Entry price: Initial profit target price: Initial stop loss price: Position size calculation:
facts.claim: The plan fields: entry price, initial target, initial stop and the position size.

facts.quote: Realized gain/loss: Grade how closely the trade plan was followed:
facts.claim: After the trade: the realized gain or loss, and a grade for how closely you followed the plan.

facts.quote: What worked? What didn't work? Lessons learned?
facts.claim: Each trade closes with what worked, what didn't and the lessons learned.

facts.quote: Keep a detailed record of your trading activity, including entry and exit points, your reasons for taking the trade, and the outcomes.
facts.claim: Record entry and exit points, your reasons for the trade, and the outcome.

facts.quote: Evaluating and reviewing your past trades will allow you to identify patterns, strengths, and areas for improvement.
facts.claim: Reviewing past trades shows your patterns, strengths and weak spots.

facts.claim: Write your conclusions in the journal so you can go back to them later.

facts.quote: Hindsight bias describes our inclination, after an event has occurred, to see the event as having been predictable, even if there had been little to no objective basis for predicting it.
facts.claim: After the fact, an event looks predictable even when there was little basis to predict it.

facts.quote: Journal entries are sometimes detailed, sometimes sketchy. They are sometimes more frequent, sometimes less frequent. The trader lacks a consistent journaling process.

facts.quote: The journal might focus on entries and exits, but not position and risk management. It is uncanny that the areas left out of journals are often those most important to work on!
facts.claim: Journals often skip position size and risk, and what gets left out is often what matters most.

facts.quote: You don't want journaling to become unduly burdensome
facts.claim: Journaling shouldn't become a burden.

facts.quote: Your journal will track how well you follow these rules, not just whether you make money or not.
facts.claim: The journal tracks how well you follow your rules, not only whether you made money.

facts.quote: it allows you to tag content and acts as a searchable database. That allows you to pull out all entries on a particular stock or all posts that pertain to a given topic, such as overtrading.

facts.quote: You can even use your phone as a scanner, take pictures of something from your trading screen, and save them to your Evernote journal.
facts.claim: You can save pictures of your trading screen in the journal.

facts.quote: Such a journal would consist of multiple charts, as well as commentary. Actual trades logged during the market day would also be depicted, along with comments on the strengths and weaknesses of the trades.
facts.claim: A strong journal has charts with the trades marked on them, plus comments.

facts.quote: Most written journals are mere summaries of a trading day or week.
facts.claim: Most written journals just summarize the day or week.

facts.quote: He makes effective use of tags to categorize his trades, enabling him to quickly identify the types of trades and markets that are working best for him.
facts.claim: Tagging trades by type shows quickly which kinds of trades work best.

facts.quote: The best journals, I find, don't make the collection of information burdensome and focus on concrete goals for improvement.
facts.claim: The best journals keep data collection light.

facts.quote: In the end, trading journals are like exercise equipment: they only produce results if you work them regularly.
facts.claim: A journal only helps if you keep it up.

facts.quote: Journal entries can be both qualitative (written summaries of the day's trading strengths and weaknesses) and quantitative (summaries of performance metrics, including P/L, number of winning/losing trades, etc.)
facts.claim: Entries hold both written notes and numbers like P&L and wins and losses.

facts.quote: The idea is to use the journal to keep a real time record of what you're thinking and feeling, so that you can become a better self-observer.
facts.claim: Recording what you think and feel makes you better at watching yourself.

facts.quote: Worry, physical tension, and feelings of nervousness are great clues to track in a journal. Once you recognize your fear patterns, you can take some deep breaths, calm yourself, and focus on assessing opportunity
facts.claim: Worry and nervousness are clues worth logging; once you see a fear pattern you can work on it.

facts.quote: They are a way of focusing on process, rather than anchoring our moods and self-esteem to the ups and downs of P/L.
facts.claim: A journal keeps your focus on process instead of the swings in P&L.

facts.quote: at the time you enter any trade, you should pre-determine some point at which you’ll get out of the trade to preserve your capital. That exit point is the risk you have in the trade or your expected loss.
facts.claim: Set your exit point when you enter. That point is your risk on the trade.

facts.quote: If you get out when it drops to $30, your loss is much bigger than 1R. It’s twice what you were planning to lose, or 2R.
facts.claim: Getting out past your planned stop makes the loss bigger than 1R; twice the planned loss is 2R.

facts.quote: A term used to express the initial risk taken in a given position, as defined by one’s initial stop loss.
facts.claim: R is the initial risk, set by your initial stop.

facts.quote: All profits and losses can be expressed as a multiple of the initial risk (R) taken.
facts.claim: Every result can be stated in R, a multiple of the initial risk.

facts.quote: At a minimum, do a brain dump, writing out everything in your mind, what happened, what the emotion was, what the trigger was, any other key details of the hand/trade/situation that can easily get lost.
facts.claim: After the session, write down what happened, the emotion, and what triggered it.

facts.quote: Details can disappear from memory and they can be the key to solving the problem and minimizing the chance it’s going to happen again.
facts.claim: Details fade from memory, and they can be what solves the problem.

facts.quote: To get started, I suggest committing to a two to four week period of time where you’ll journal 3 – 5 minutes each time.
facts.claim: Start with short sessions: 3 to 5 minutes each time.

facts.quote: What mistakes did you make? How can you improve on them and/or be better next time?
facts.claim: Close the review with your mistakes and how to do better next time.

facts.quote: Kahneman uses prospect theory to highlight biases of judgment—overconfidence, optimism, hindsight, and overreaction to past events
facts.claim: Hindsight is one of investors' known biases of judgment.

facts.quote: These errors and biases lead to poor investment decisions.
facts.claim: Those biases lead to poor investment decisions.

facts.quote: The disposition effect is the tendency of investors to sell winning positions
facts.claim: Investors tend to sell their winning positions; this is called the disposition effect.

facts.quote: demonstrating that the disposition effect is widely operative and that this investment strategy is counterproductive
facts.claim: Odean found the habit is widespread and counterproductive.

facts.quote: Drawdowns (maximum loss per trade using a trading system)
facts.claim: CME lists drawdowns, the maximum loss per trade, among what your records should let you analyze.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: Rule A4: our stop only moves up, never down or wider; a gap against the stop is the one exception.

facts.quote: Journal every trade the same day and review the week every weekend, ideally.
facts.claim: Rule B27: we journal every trade the same day and review the week every weekend, ideally.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: Rule C28: we never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: Rule B22: no new buys in the 3 days before earnings, and hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.

facts.quote: Every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the market opens.
facts.claim: Rule D39: every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the market opens.

facts.quote: Each month, review the numbers: win rate, average win and loss in R, expectancy, and other statistics.
facts.claim: Rule E59: each month we review win rate, average win and loss in R, and expectancy.

walkthroughs.title: Same fields, every trade
steps: Most journals are summaries of the day. One entry is detailed, the next is sketchy, and none of it sorts.
So log every trade in the same fixed fields. Schwab's worksheet works that way: one sheet, filled out for each trade.
Fixed fields and tags can be sorted. Then every trade of one kind comes up at once.

walkthroughs.title: Before the click, after the close
steps: Before you buy, log the date and the plan: why you're taking it, entry, stop, target and size.
Write the reason now. After the fact, the trade looks easier to call than it was.
After you close, log the result: the exit, the R it made, and how closely you followed the plan.
Finish with what worked, what didn't, and one lesson.

walkthroughs.title: Tags and a picture
steps: Tag the setup, the emotion and any mistake from a short list. Use the same word every time.
Save the chart when you enter, with your levels marked.
Keep it short enough to do on every trade. A journal only works if you keep working it.

questions.q: Why log every trade in the same fixed fields instead of free notes?
choices: So you can sort and compare trades
So entries are longer and richer
So you can skip written notes
So you can fill it in weekly
questions.answer: So you can sort and compare trades
questions.why: So you can sort and compare trades. Free notes drift: detailed one day, sketchy the next. Schwab notes that a spreadsheet lets you track, sort and analyze. Steenbarger says tags pull up every entry on one stock or one topic. Fixed fields do not mean longer entries or no written notes. The reason and the lesson are fields too.
questions.lesson_line: Same fields on every trade. That's what makes a journal you can sort.

wrong.So entries are longer and richer: Longer isn't the goal. The best journals keep collecting the information light.
wrong.So you can skip written notes: The reason and the lesson are fields too. A good entry holds numbers and written notes.
wrong.So you can fill it in weekly: Fixed fields are about what you log, not when. CME Group says to record why as you enter. Our rule: journal every trade the same day, ideally.

questions.simple: Fixed fields let you sort and compare your trades, so every trade of one kind comes up at once.

questions.q: The best time to log why you took a trade is after it closes, when you know how it went.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Write the reason as you enter the trade, as CME Group advises. After an event, people tend to see it as predictable, even with little basis to predict it. That is hindsight bias, one of the known biases of judgment. A note written at entry keeps what you really thought. The result goes in after the close. The reason does not.
questions.lesson_line: Log the reason before the result. Afterwards, hindsight edits it.
questions.simple: False. Write the reason as you enter, because after the close the trade looks easier to call than it was.

questions.q: A useful log entry holds two kinds of information. Which two?
choices: Numbers and your written reasons
Your P&L and account balance
Price alerts and news headlines
Winning and losing trades
questions.answer: Numbers and your written reasons
questions.why: Numbers and your written reasons. Steenbarger says entries can be quantitative, like P&L and wins and losses, and qualitative, like written summaries. Investopedia lists entry and exit points beside your reasons for taking the trade. Numbers show what happened. Your words show why. Every trade, win or loss, holds both.
questions.lesson_line: Numbers say what happened. Your notes say why. Log both.

wrong.Your P&L and account balance: Both are numbers. Neither says why you took the trade or how you ran it.
wrong.Price alerts and news headlines: Those come from the market. Your log records what you decided and why.
wrong.Winning and losing trades: That sorts trades by result, not by kind of information. Every entry, win or loss, holds numbers and your reasons.

questions.simple: A good entry holds numbers and your written reasons, because numbers show what happened and your words show why.

questions.q: Which field does this note belong in?
questions.sentence: 'Nervous all day, checked the quote every minute' goes in the ___ field.
questions.answer: emotion
questions.why: Emotion. The note describes a feeling, nervousness, and the habit it drove. Steenbarger calls worry, physical tension and nervousness great clues to track in a journal. Tendler says to write down what the emotion was and what triggered it. In their own field, feelings can be lined up against your trades.
questions.lesson_line: Feelings get their own field. That's how a fear pattern shows up.
questions.simple: It goes in the emotion field, because nervous feelings are clues worth tracking next to what you did.

questions.q: 'Bought because it cleared a six-week base on heavy volume.' Which field holds this?
choices: Reason for the trade
Lesson for next time
Exit plan for the trade
Emotion at the entry
questions.answer: Reason for the trade
questions.why: Reason for the trade. The note says why you bought: the base and the volume. CME Group says to record why you made the trade as you enter it. Investopedia lists your reasons for taking the trade as part of the record. A lesson comes after the result, and an exit plan says where you get out.
questions.lesson_line: Why you bought is its own field, written before you know the outcome.

wrong.Lesson for next time: A lesson is what you take from the result. This note gives the reason you bought.
wrong.Exit plan for the trade: An exit plan says where you'd get out. This note says why you got in.
wrong.Emotion at the entry: There's no feeling in it. It's a chart reason: the base and the volume.

questions.simple: It is the reason for the trade, because it says why you bought, and you write that as you enter.

questions.q: At the end of the day, adding up your P&L is the most important part of your log.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. CME Group says adding up your profit or loss is secondary to knowing the why and how of your trading. Steenbarger says a journal keeps your focus on process, not on the ups and downs of P&L. The total still goes in the log. It is just not the main thing you review.
questions.lesson_line: The total is the easy part. The why and the how are what you review.
questions.simple: False, because the total is the easy part, and knowing why and how you traded matters more.

questions.q: Finish the last field of a log entry.
questions.sentence: What worked, what didn't, and the ___ for next time.
questions.answer: lesson
questions.why: Lesson. Schwab's worksheet ends each trade with three lines: what worked, what didn't work, and lessons learned. Tendler closes a review the same way: your mistakes, and how to be better next time. Profit is a result field and the target is a plan field. Neither is the lesson.
questions.lesson_line: Every entry ends with one lesson you can use tomorrow.
questions.simple: The last field is the lesson, the one thing you will do better next time.

questions.q: Which field shows you broke your rules, even on a trade that made money?
choices: Your grade for following the plan
Realized gain or loss in dollars
Exit price on the closing fill
Planned target price for the trade
questions.answer: Your grade for following the plan
questions.why: The plan grade. Schwab's worksheet has its own line to grade how closely the plan was followed, next to the realized gain or loss. Steenbarger says the journal tracks how well you follow your rules, not just whether you make money. A broken rule can still pay. The P&L, the exit and the target cannot show it. Only the grade does.
questions.lesson_line: Grade the plan apart from the P&L. A broken rule that paid is still broken.

wrong.Realized gain or loss in dollars: P&L shows the result, not how you got it. A rule break can still make money.
wrong.Exit price on the closing fill: The exit says where you got out. It can't say whether that was the plan.
wrong.Planned target price for the trade: That's part of the plan itself. It can't say whether you stuck to it.

questions.simple: The plan grade shows it, because a trade can make money even when you broke your rules.

reasons: fixed before (stem and a distractor changed 2026-11-09)

questions.q: Which of these goes in the log before you click buy?
choices: Entry, stop, target and size
Exit price and the R made
What worked, what didn't
The realized gain or loss
questions.answer: Entry, stop, target and size
questions.why: Entry, stop, target and size. Those are the plan fields, and they go in before the trade. Schwab's worksheet lists entry price, initial profit target, initial stop loss and position size. Tharp says to set your exit point at the time you enter any trade. Our rule: every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the market opens. The exit, the R and the review come after you close.
questions.lesson_line: Plan fields before the click. Result fields after the close.

wrong.Exit price and the R made: You don't have those until the trade is over. They're result fields.
wrong.What worked, what didn't: That's the review at the end. You can't answer it before the trade.
wrong.The realized gain or loss: Realized means the trade is closed. That comes last, in the result fields.

questions.simple: The plan goes in first: entry, stop, target and size, because the rest only exists once the trade is closed.

questions.q: Your log: entry $40, initial stop $39, exit $41.50. What R goes in the result field?
questions.why: 1.5R. R is the initial risk, set by your initial stop: from $40 down to $39. The gain ran from $40 up to $41.50, one and a half times that distance. Van Tharp's glossary says every profit or loss can be stated as a multiple of that initial risk.
questions.lesson_line: Log every result in R, measured against the initial stop.
questions.simple: Log 1.5R, because the gain was one and a half times the risk from entry to the initial stop.

questions.q: A log that covers your entries and exits covers what you most need to fix.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Steenbarger warns that a journal might focus on entries and exits, but not position and risk management. He adds that the areas left out are often the ones most important to work on. Schwab's worksheet gives the initial stop and the position size their own lines. CME Group wants records that show your drawdowns, the maximum loss per trade.
questions.lesson_line: If size and stop aren't fields, your log can't show the mistakes in them.
questions.simple: False, because logs often skip how you manage the position and the risk, and those often matter most.

questions.story: Three of your notes say 'chased it,' 'FOMO buy' and 'bought way up.' You want to know what chasing costs you.
questions.q: What makes that quick to check?
choices: Giving every chase one fixed tag
Writing longer notes on every trade
Rereading all of your old notes
Logging only the trades you chase
questions.answer: Giving every chase one fixed tag
questions.why: Give every chase one fixed tag. Three names for one mistake will not sort together. Use the same tag word every time, and one search pulls up every chase. Steenbarger says tags turn a journal into a searchable database, by stock or by topic, such as overtrading. Schwab notes a spreadsheet lets you sort and analyze. Then the chases can be compared with the rest.
questions.lesson_line: One mistake, one tag, the same word every time.

wrong.Writing longer notes on every trade: More words, same problem. Three names for one mistake still won't sort together.
wrong.Rereading all of your old notes: It works, slowly, and you redo it each time you want the answer. A fixed tag answers it in one search.
wrong.Logging only the trades you chase: Then you can't compare chases with your other trades. Every trade goes in the log.

questions.simple: Give every chase the same tag, because one word can be searched and sorted, and three different words cannot.

deeper.example: Keep a short list of mistake tags and pick the words once. Here the word could be chased. Every entry that bought far above the plan gets that tag, never FOMO one day and bought way up the next. One filter then shows how those trades did next to all the rest. Never invent a new word for an old mistake.

questions.q: A log of just the ticker and P&L for each trade can tell you which setup works.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. A ticker and a P&L cannot tell you the setup. You need a setup field or tag on every trade. CME Group wants records that show profit or loss for a particular system or strategy. Steenbarger describes tags that quickly show which types of trades work best.
questions.lesson_line: No setup field, no setup stats. Tag it on every trade.
questions.simple: False, because without the setup on every trade, the log has no way to group results by setup.

questions.q: Your plan said buy at $50. You filled at $51. How far above plan was the fill, in percent?
questions.why: 2%. Measure the gap from the planned $50 to the $51 fill, as a share of the planned $50. Log the planned entry and the real fill as two fields. Schwab's review asks whether your entries were performed effectively, and these two fields answer it.
questions.lesson_line: Log the planned entry and the real fill. The gap is your execution.
questions.simple: The fill was 2% above plan, because the gap from $50 to $51 is 2% of the planned price.

deeper.example: Our rule sets a line for this gap: never buy more than 4% above the buy point. If $50 was your buy point, a $51 fill is inside it. Logging both prices on every trade is how you see whether you stay inside the line, trade after trade.

questions.story: You bought at $20 with a stop at $19. It slid, so you moved the stop to $18. It hit there.
questions.q: What R goes in your log?
choices: A loss of 2R on the trade
A loss of 1R on it
A loss of 0.5R on it
No R, the plan changed
questions.answer: A loss of 2R on the trade
questions.why: A loss of 2R. R is the initial risk, set by your initial stop: $20 down to $19. You got out at $18, twice that distance. Tharp says getting out past your planned stop makes the loss bigger than 1R. Twice the plan is 2R. Moving the stop does not reset R. Our rule: the stop only moves up, never down, with one exception for a gap.
questions.lesson_line: R is set at entry. Moving the stop changes the loss, not the yardstick.

wrong.A loss of 1R on it: That measures from the moved stop. Your planned risk was $20 to $19, and you lost twice that.
wrong.A loss of 0.5R on it: That flips the math. R is the loss divided by the planned risk, not the planned risk divided by the loss.
wrong.No R, the plan changed: That's exactly the trade your log needs to show. Measure it against the stop you set at entry.

questions.simple: Log a 2R loss, because R comes from the stop you set at entry, and moving the stop does not change it.

deeper.trap: The trap is to log the loss against the stop you moved to. That makes a 2R loss look like 1R, and the log hides the rule you broke. Keep the initial stop in its own field and never edit it. Then a stop moved down and hit shows up as a loss bigger than 1R, and your review can count them.

questions.story: Your emotion field says 'anxious' on 7 of your last 8 early exits. All 8 stocks went on to hit your target.
questions.q: What is your log telling you?
choices: Fear is cutting your winners short
Your targets are set too far away
Those exits were sound risk control
Feelings are noise, drop that field
questions.answer: Fear is cutting your winners short
questions.why: Fear is cutting your winners short. The emotion field says anxious on 7 of 8 early exits, and each stock went on to hit your target. Steenbarger calls worry and nervousness clues to track. Once you see a fear pattern, you can work on it. A report for the SEC describes the disposition effect: investors tend to sell winning positions and hold onto losing ones. Odean found it widespread and counterproductive. A planned sale is not this. A sale out of fear, before your plan, is.
questions.lesson_line: Same feeling on the same mistake is a pattern. The emotion field is how you find it.

wrong.Your targets are set too far away: The stocks reached your targets. The targets were fine. The exits weren't.
wrong.Those exits were sound risk control: Your stop is your risk control. These exits came early, out of anxiety, on trades that went on to work.
wrong.Feelings are noise, drop that field: That field is what found the pattern. Without it you'd see early exits, not why.

questions.simple: Fear is making you sell too soon, because the same anxious feeling shows up on nearly every early exit.

deeper.trap: The trap is to judge each early exit alone. One exit before the target can be a fair call. 7 of 8 with the same feeling is a pattern. Only an emotion field filled in every time lets you see it. And a target hit later does not prove any single exit was wrong. The pattern is the point.

questions.story: A stock you bought a month ago has doubled. You remember buying it as a long-term leader. Your log, written at entry, says 'quick trade into earnings.'
questions.q: Which do you go by in your review?
choices: The log you wrote when you bought
Your memory, it knows the story
Neither, the profit is what counts
Whichever fits how it turned out
questions.answer: The log you wrote when you bought
questions.why: The log you wrote when you bought. You wrote it before you knew the ending. After an event, people tend to see it as more predictable than it was. That is hindsight bias. Your review grades the plan you really had, a quick trade into earnings, not the story you remember now.
questions.lesson_line: Trust what you wrote before you knew the ending.

wrong.Your memory, it knows the story: Memory knows the ending, and that's the problem. After the fact, events look more predictable than they were.
wrong.Neither, the profit is what counts: The profit is real, but the plan was a quick trade. Your review needs to see that.
wrong.Whichever fits how it turned out: That's hindsight bias doing the review for you.

questions.simple: Go by the log, because you wrote it before you knew the ending, and memory rewrites the story.

deeper.example: The log also lets the review test the plan against our rules. Our rule: no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. Hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R. A note that says quick trade into earnings tells you which rule to check. Memory would have quietly dropped it.

questions.story: Your journal template asks 40 questions per trade. Two weeks in, you've stopped filling it out.
questions.q: What's the best fix?
choices: Cut it to a few fixed fields
Force yourself through all 40
Log only your biggest losers
Stop until your trading improves
questions.answer: Cut it to a few fixed fields
questions.why: Cut it to a few fixed fields. Steenbarger says the best journals don't make collecting information burdensome, and journaling shouldn't become a burden. Tendler suggests starting with 3 to 5 minutes each time. A journal only works if you keep working it. Our rule is to journal every trade the same day, ideally, and a short form makes that doable.
questions.lesson_line: A short log you fill every time beats a long one you quit.

wrong.Force yourself through all 40: Willpower won't fix a form that's too long. The same thing happens again.
wrong.Log only your biggest losers: That skips trades instead of fixing the form. The fix is fewer fields, not fewer trades.
wrong.Stop until your trading improves: That's when the journal helps most. A journal only works if you keep working it.

questions.simple: Cut the form to a few fixed fields, because a short log you fill every time beats a long one you quit.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking more questions make a better journal. A 40-question form gets skipped, and a skipped entry teaches nothing. Keep the plan fields, the result, the plan grade, one lesson and a few tags. That is enough to sort your trades and find the patterns.

questions.story: A month later you review a loss. Your note says 'bought the breakout over my line.' You never logged where the line was.
questions.q: What would have shown you where the line was?
choices: A chart saved at entry, line marked
Today's chart, line drawn from memory
The final P&L recorded on the trade
The news headlines from that day
questions.answer: A chart saved at entry, line marked
questions.why: A chart saved at entry, with the line marked. CME Group lists support and resistance levels among what to record as you enter. Steenbarger notes you can save pictures of your trading screen in the journal. Tendler warns that details fade from memory, and they can be the key to the problem. A chart drawn today is drawn by someone who knows the ending.
questions.lesson_line: Save the chart when you enter, with your levels on it. A picture beats a memory.

wrong.Today's chart, line drawn from memory: Now you know how it ended, so the line lands wherever fits the story.
wrong.The final P&L recorded on the trade: The P&L says it lost. It says nothing about where your line was.
wrong.The news headlines from that day: News might explain the move. It can't show where your line was.

questions.simple: A chart saved when you bought, with the line marked, because a picture keeps the level that memory loses.

deeper.trap: The trap is redrawing the line today. Once you know how the trade ended, the line tends to land wherever fits the story. Save the chart at entry, with the line marked, before the result exists. Then the review judges the line you really had.

questions.story: Your log keeps a planned entry and an actual fill. On 8 of your last 10 trades, the fill was 5% to 8% above the plan.
questions.q: What is the log showing you?
choices: You keep chasing past the plan
Your planned entries are too low
Normal slippage, nothing to fix
Your stops are set too tight
questions.answer: You keep chasing past the plan
questions.why: You keep chasing past the plan. On 8 of your last 10 trades, the fill was 5% to 8% above the planned entry. Our rule: never buy more than 4% above the buy point, and these fills went past it. Schwab's review asks whether your entries were performed effectively, and this log says no. Investopedia says reviewing past trades shows your patterns. Fix the click, not the plan.
questions.lesson_line: Plan and fill side by side. When the fill keeps running ahead of the plan, fix the click, not the plan.

wrong.Your planned entries are too low: That bends the plan to fit the habit. The plan was the level. The fills drifted.
wrong.Normal slippage, nothing to fix: A small miss now and then is normal. 5% to 8% above plan on 8 of 10 trades is past our 4% line, and a habit.
wrong.Your stops are set too tight: Nothing here is about stops. The gap is between the planned entry and the fill.

questions.simple: You are chasing, because on most trades you paid more than 4% over your planned price, past our line.

deeper.trap: The trap is moving the plan up to meet the fills. Then the log looks clean and the habit hides. Keep the planned entry fixed, log the real fill beside it, and compare the two when you review. Our rule is to review the week every weekend, ideally.

questions.story: To save time, you log only the trades that go wrong. Now you want your win rate and your best setup.
questions.q: What can this log tell you?
choices: Neither one, the winners are missing
Both, once you log enough losers
Your win rate, from the losers alone
The best setup, by its smallest losses
questions.answer: Neither one, the winners are missing
questions.why: Neither one. A win rate is the share of your trades that made money versus those that didn't, so it needs every trade. Profit or loss by setup needs the winners too. CME Group wants the why and how of your wins, not only your losses. Our rule is to journal every trade the same day, ideally.
questions.lesson_line: Log every trade, winners too. A log of losers can't tell you what works.

wrong.Both, once you log enough losers: More losers never add the winners. A win rate needs every trade, and a best setup needs its wins.
wrong.Your win rate, from the losers alone: You'd need the total number of trades. Without the winners, you don't have it.
wrong.The best setup, by its smallest losses: Small losses don't make a setup the best. A setup earns that with its wins, and those aren't in this log.

questions.simple: Neither, because a win rate and a best setup both need your winning trades, and this log left them out.

deeper.trap: The trap feels efficient: losers teach the most, so log only those. But a log of losers can't even tell you how often you lose. A setup missing from it may be one you rarely trade, not one that works. Every trade goes in, winners too.

questions.q: Under our rule, when do you journal a trade, and when do you review?
choices: Same day, then review each weekend
Each weekend, then review monthly
Same day, then review each quarter
Each month, then review each quarter
questions.answer: Same day, then review each weekend
questions.why: Same day, then review each weekend. Our rule: journal every trade the same day and review the week every weekend, ideally. Schwab suggests a review at the end of the month or quarter. Where our rulebook speaks, we follow it. Details fade from memory, so the same day is when you still have them.
questions.lesson_line: Log it the same day. Review the week on the weekend.
questions.simple: Journal each trade the same day and review the week every weekend. That is our rule, ideally.

wrong.Each weekend, then review monthly: That waits too long to log. Our rule journals every trade the same day, ideally.
wrong.Same day, then review each quarter: The logging is right, the review is late. Our rule reviews the week every weekend, ideally.
wrong.Each month, then review each quarter: Both wait too long. Our rule: journal the same day and review the week every weekend.

deeper.example: The weekend review reads the week's entries. Our rule adds a monthly look at the numbers: win rate, average win and loss in R, and expectancy. Fixed fields make both reviews quick.
